title: Labyrinthus. Ariadnes corona
titleEn: The Labyrinth and Ariadne's Crown — Metamorphoses VIII.152–182
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Minos comes home to Crete, pays his hundred bulls to Jove, and finds the disgrace of his house grown into a body: a creature half bull and half man, born of his wife's adultery. He has Daedalus build a house of blind winding halls to shut it in, and there the monster is fed on Athenian blood until the third drawing of lots brings the man who masters it — the son of Aegeus, who sails away with the king's daughter and then leaves her on the shore of Dia. Bacchus comes to her there, and the crown he takes from her forehead is thrown into the sky, where its gems settle into fire between two constellations.

sentences.t:
Vota Iovi Minos taurorum corpora centum
solvit, ut egressus ratibus Curetida terram
contigit, spoliis decorata est regia fixis.
sentences.l: His vows to Jove Minos discharged — a hundred bodies of bulls — as soon as, disembarked from his ships, he touched the Curetes' land; with spoils nailed up the palace was adorned.
sentences.i: Minos discharged his vows to Jove with a hundred bulls' bodies, the moment he stepped off his ships onto the land of the Curetes; and the palace was hung about with the spoils, nailed up.
sentences.n: vota solvere is the set phrase for discharging a vow — paying what was promised — and taurorum corpora centum stands in apposition to Vota, so the vow and the hundred bulls that pay it are named as one thing. Curetida is the Greek form of the accusative singular (Curetis, -idos), a feminine adjective agreeing with terram — the Curetes' land, that is Crete, named after the Curetes, who were said to have guarded the infant Jupiter there. It is a Greek ending on a plain object, not the Greek accusative of respect. ut with the perfect contigit means “as soon as”, not “in order that”. One thing about the text itself: line 154 as printed here, contigit, spoliis decorata est regia fixis, is a syllable short and will not scan — the second foot would have to open on the short first syllable of spoliis. Other editions print et spoliis, which restores both the metre and the connective. The line is given exactly as the edition prints it and nothing has been added to it.

sentences.t:
Creverat opprobrium generis, foedumque patebat
matris adulterium monstri novitate biformis.
sentences.l: The disgrace of the stock had grown, and foul stood open to view the mother's adultery, through the strangeness of the two-formed monster.
sentences.i: The disgrace of the line had grown, and the mother's foul adultery lay exposed in the strangeness of that two-shaped monster.
sentences.n: These lines name neither the mother nor the bull: the whole of the affair is matris adulterium, “the mother's adultery”, with the monster's double shape standing as the proof. adulterium is a word of blame and it is kept as blame in both layers; the offence is registered as opprobrium generis, a disgrace to the family line — that is, to Minos. foedum is split from its noun adulterium across the line break, so the ugliness is stated before the thing that is ugly. biformis is “of two shapes”, and novitas is strangeness and newness at once: the creature is unheard-of as well as monstrous.

sentences.t:
Destinat hunc Minos thalamo removere pudorem
multiplicique domo caecisque includere tectis.
sentences.l: Minos resolves to remove this shame from his chamber and to shut it in a many-folded house and in blind halls.
sentences.i: Minos determined to put this shame out of his own bedchamber and lock it away in a house of many turnings, in halls that were blind.
sentences.n: pudorem here is a thing, not a feeling: “this shame” is the creature itself, the object of removere. thalamo is an ablative of separation — out of the marriage-chamber, and so out of the marriage. caeca tecta, “blind halls”: caecus of a place means both unlit and giving no sight of the way through, and Latin uses the word of the one who cannot see and of the thing that cannot be seen alike. multiplici domo is “a house of many folds”, the building described before it is named.

sentences.t:
Daedalus ingenio fabrae celeberrimus artis
ponit opus turbatque notas et lumina flexu
ducit in errorem variarum ambage viarum.
sentences.l: Daedalus, most renowned in genius for the craftsman's art, lays down the work, and confuses the marks, and leads the eyes into wandering by the bend, by the roundabout of manifold ways.
sentences.i: Daedalus, the most celebrated genius the builder's craft had, laid out the work: he muddled the signs, and by curve after curve, by the going-round of ways that never ran the same, he drew the eye off into error.
sentences.n: ingenio is an ablative of respect with celeberrimus, “most renowned in genius”, and fabrae artis is a genitive depending on it: genius in the craftsman's art. notas are the marks a traveller steers by, and turbat is to throw them into confusion. errorem is “wandering” before it is “mistake”, and the two senses run together through the whole passage that follows. ambage is the ablative of ambages, a going-round. Magnus prints flexu, an ablative, “by the bend”; some editions print flexum, which attaches the bending to errorem instead and makes the wandering curve rather than the road.

sentences.t:
Non secus ac liquidis Phrygius Maeandrus in undis
ludit et ambiguo lapsu refluitque fluitque
occurrensque sibi venturas adspicit undas,
et nunc ad fontes, nunc ad mare versus apertum
incertas exercet aquas: ita Daedalus implet
innumeras errore vias.
sentences.l: Not otherwise than as the Phrygian Maeander plays in its clear waters and with a doubtful gliding flows back and flows on, and, running to meet itself, looks upon waters that are still to come, and, turned now toward its springs, now toward the open sea, drives its uncertain waters — so Daedalus fills countless ways with wandering.
sentences.i: Just as the Phrygian Maeander plays in its clear water and, gliding either way, runs back and runs on, and, coming up against itself, watches water that has not arrived yet, and, facing now its own springs and now the open sea, keeps its undecided current at work — so Daedalus filled path after path, past counting, with going astray.
sentences.n: The sentence is built to be hard to get out of: five verbs of the simile — ludit, refluit, fluit, adspicit, exercet — go past before ita arrives and tells the reader what the comparison was for. refluit is put before fluit, so the river flows back before it flows on. occurrens sibi is the river meeting its own stream at a bend, which is why the water it “sees coming” is water it has already carried past. versus is the perfect participle of verto agreeing with Maeandrus, “turned toward”, not the preposition that looks the same. Magnus prints liquidis Phrygius Maeandrus in undis, “the Phrygian Maeander in its clear waters”; some editions read liquidus Phrygiis Maeandros in arvis, which makes the river itself clear and sets it in Phrygian fields.

sentences.t:
Vixque ipse reverti
ad limen potuit: tanta est fallacia tecti.
sentences.l: And scarcely could he himself return to the threshold: so great is the trickery of the house.
sentences.i: And he himself could barely find his way back to the door: such is the deceit of that building.
sentences.n: reverti is the present infinitive of revertor, a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning, “to turn back”. The tenses shift under the reader here: implet in the line before and est at the end are present, potuit between them is perfect, and this alternation of historic present with perfect is one of the poem's ways of changing speed. fallacia is the noun from fallo, “to deceive”: the building's power to mislead, not a quality of the man who built it.

sentences.t:
Quo postquam geminam tauri iuvenisque figuram
clausit, et Actaeo bis pastum sanguine monstrum
tertia sors annis domuit repetita novenis,
sentences.l: And after he had shut up in it the twin shape of bull and of youth, and the third drawing of lots, repeated at each ninth year, had mastered the monster twice fed on Attic blood,
sentences.i: And once he had closed inside it that double shape, bull and young man in one, and the third drawing of lots — it came round every ninth year — had put down the monster twice fed on Athenian blood,
sentences.n: Quo is a connecting relative in the ablative, “and in it”, meaning the labyrinth; Latin opens the sentence with the pronoun where English wants “And after he had shut…”. sors is the drawing of lots: Athens owed Crete a tribute of young people chosen by lot, and “twice fed on Attic blood” counts the two earlier drawings, so the third is the one still to come. Actaeus is “Attic”, from Acte, an old name for the land of Athens. annis novenis uses the distributive numeral novenus, so this is an interval — at each ninth year — and not a stretch of nine. domuit takes sors as its subject by a compression: it is the drawing that brings the man who masters the monster, and the poem does not stop to say so. pastum is a perfect participle agreeing with monstrum.

sentences.t:
utque ope virginea nullis iterata priorum
ianua difficilis filo est inventa relecto,
sentences.l: and when, by a maiden's help, the difficult doorway, retraced by none of those before, was found by means of the thread gathered up again,
sentences.i: and when a girl's help found that hard doorway once more — a doorway none before had ever retraced — by the thread taken back up along the way,
sentences.n: ope virginea is a girl's help: Ariadne's, though she is named only two lines later, and then only as Minois, “Minos's daughter”. nullis priorum is a dative of the agent with the perfect participle iterata, which is the normal construction after such a participle: “retraced by none of the earlier ones”. They had gone in; none had come back over the same ground. relego means both “to gather up again” and “to travel over again”, so filo relecto is at once the string wound back onto the spool and the road walked a second time, and the double sense is the whole of the trick.

sentences.t:
protinus Aegides rapta Minoide Diam
vela dedit comitemque suam crudelis in illo
litore destituit.
sentences.l: at once the son of Aegeus, with Minos's daughter carried off, gave his sails to Dia, and, cruel, on that shore abandoned the companion who was his own.
sentences.i: then at once the son of Aegeus, having carried Minos's daughter off with him, set sail for Dia — and there, cruel, left on that shore the companion who was his own.
sentences.n: rapta Minoide is an ablative absolute, “with the daughter of Minos carried off”. Both people in the sentence are named by descent and not by name: Aegides, “son of Aegeus”, and Minois, “daughter of Minos”, so the girl who saved him is identified by the father whose monster he had come to kill. crudelis is a nominative adjective standing on the subject, not an adverb — the poem calls Theseus cruel rather than saying he acted cruelly, and the judgement is the poem's own, not a character's. Diam is a bare accusative of destination after vela dedit, with no preposition, which verse allows with place-names; Dia is the island commonly identified with Naxos. suam is emphatic: his own companion.

sentences.t:
Desertae et multa querenti
amplexus et opem Liber tulit;
sentences.l: To her, abandoned and complaining of much, Liber brought embraces and help;
sentences.i: Liber came to the girl left there, complaining and complaining, and brought her his embrace and his help;
sentences.n: Desertae and querenti are both datives, both feminine, both Ariadne, and neither is a name. querenti is the present participle of queror, a deponent — passive in form, active in meaning, “complaining”. multa is a neuter plural accusative used as an internal object: complaining many things, complaint after complaint. amplexus is the accusative plural of the fourth-declension noun amplexus, “embraces”, not a participle of amplector, which the form also looks like. Liber is the Roman name for Bacchus.

sentences.t:
utque perenni
sidere clara foret, sumptam de fronte coronam
inmisit caelo.
sentences.l: and so that she might be bright with an unfailing constellation, the crown, taken from her brow, he sent up into the sky.
sentences.i: and so that she should shine with a constellation that never fails, he sent the crown, lifted from her forehead, into the sky.
sentences.n: foret is an old form of esset, imperfect subjunctive, here in a purpose clause after ut. sidere is ablative, and sidus is a constellation rather than a single star, which matters, because what goes up is a whole circle of gems. sumptam is a perfect participle agreeing with coronam with no agent expressed, so the Latin does not say whose hand took the crown from her forehead, hers or his. caelo is dative after inmisit, “sent into the sky”.

sentences.t:
Tenues volat illa per auras
dumque volat, gemmae nitidos vertuntur in ignes
consistuntque loco specie remanente coronae,
qui medius Nixique genu est anguemque tenentis.
sentences.l: It flies through the thin breezes, and while it flies the gems are turned into gleaming fires and take their stand in a place, with the look of a crown remaining — a place which is midway between the one who has knelt on his knee and the one holding the snake.
sentences.i: The crown flies through the thin air, and as it flies the gems turn into bright fires and settle in one place, still keeping the shape of a crown: the place that lies between Him-on-his-knee and the man who grips the snake.
sentences.n: illa is the crown, feminine, carried over from the line before. vertuntur is passive in form, but Latin regularly uses the passive of verto of a thing turning into something else, with no agent named and none needed — “are turned into”, which is why the idiomatic layer can say that the gems turn into fires. specie remanente coronae is an ablative absolute, “with the appearance of a crown remaining”, and it is what makes the shape recognisable overhead. The last line names two constellations by description instead of by name: Nixus genu, “the one who has knelt on his knee” (nixus is the perfect participle of nitor, a deponent, active in meaning), and anguem tenens, “the one holding the snake”. The circle of fire set between them is the Northern Crown.
